title: MiaA-mediated tRNA modifications couple tryptophan attenuation and changes in tRNA abundance to complex phenotypes in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and extracted both GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) archives: GSE322698 (1.3 MB, 10 samples) and GSE323095 (2.1 MB, 16 samples). Each file is a featureCounts table with 5,966 gene rows and columns Geneid/Chr/Start/End/Strand/Length/name/count; 0 duplicate gene IDs, 0 missing values. Built the count matrix, normalised to counts per million, and found 3,775 genes expressed above 10 counts per million in both assays. Measured replicate agreement (Pearson r on log2 counts per million: 0.989-0.994 for ribosome profiling, 0.937-0.966 for RNA), split-half reliability of the translation-efficiency change (r = 0.55), then downloaded the PA14 reference coding sequences from NCBI (2.0 MB), matched 5,476/5,966 features by exact genome coordinates, computed 61 codon frequencies and ran a 5-fold cross-validated ridge regression: R-squared = 0.027 (Pearson r = 0.16); shuffled labels gave R-squared ~0.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The tryptophan-attenuation mechanism, the LC-MS (liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry) modification measurements, the Galleria mellonella (wax moth larva) infection results, the nanopore transfer-RNA sequencing, and the claim that miaA expression tracks virulence across 77 clinical isolates (virulence values come from the authors' earlier paper, not deposited here). I confirmed the proteomics deposit PXD076088 exists and is public in PRIDE (Orbitrap/MaxQuant, 'PARTIAL' submission) but did not open its files. Europe PMC's supplementary-file endpoint timed out, so the supplementary tables (S1 strains, S2 primers, S3) were not retrieved.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified: both GEO archives downloaded anonymously over FTP (3.5 MB total) and extracted; no login, no application. Nanopore transfer-RNA data (ENA projects PRJEB83028/PRJEB111160) is raw signal and excluded by our own no-raw-sequencing rule.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Raw counts are columns; the label (change in translation efficiency = ribosome footprints divided by messenger RNA, mutant minus wild type) is a derived ratio computed within one series on a clean locus-tag key - a few hours, not cross-source inference. Important caveat: the codon-resolution stalling signal the paper is actually about is NOT deposited in processed form and would need raw read reprocessing.

a3_inputs_present.note: Sequences are absent from the deposit. I fetched one 2.0 MB NCBI file (GCF_000014625.1) and mapped it by genome coordinates because the locus-tag namespaces differ (PA14_00010 in the counts vs PA14_RS00005 in RefSeq); 5,476 of 5,966 features matched exactly. One download, not thousands of lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: Verified in the files: raw read counts per feature, feature length in base pairs, and the full featureCounts command (strandedness, mapping quality 20, annotation file) recorded as a header comment in every file.

a5_enough_rows.note: 5,966 gene rows per sample; 3,775 genes pass an expression filter and carry a label. Numerically fine, but the whole table comes from one knockout-versus-wild-type contrast with 2-3 replicates per group, so the biological replication is thin.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 3.5 MB of count tables plus a 2 MB genome file
a6_fits_laptop.note: Verified: the entire analysis above, including ridge cross-validation, ran in about 2 seconds on a laptop CPU with well under 1 GB of RAM.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: No row counts are claimed in the paper to check against; GEO sample titles match the described design (wild type, delta-miaA, trpL attenuator point mutants). Minor mismatch: methods say 'at least three biological replicates', but GEO holds only 2 wild-type ribosome-profiling and 2 delta-miaA RNA samples (replicate 2 missing), consistent with quality-control dropout.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels are measured sequencing counts from featureCounts, not another model's output. Features (codon composition from the reference genome) are independent of the measurement, so no leakage by construction; the only shared term is gene length, which normalisation to counts per million and frequencies removes.

B1.why: 26 identically formatted per-sample files across two series; concatenating on Geneid worked first time, but it is not one table.

B2.why: Every file parsed first try with pandas (tab-separated, one comment header line); verified on all 26.

B3.why: Label mixes two assay types (ribosome footprints vs 3'-tag RNA) from one lab; comparable only after counts-per-million normalisation.

B4.why: No censored or qualitative values in the files; only low counts, removed by a simple expression filter.

B5.why: Verified: 0 duplicated gene IDs and 0 missing values in the 5,966-row count matrix.

B6.why: All columns documented by the featureCounts header, but sample labels like 'PL04' need the paper's methods to decode.

C1.why: I already ran the core question and got R-squared 0.027; a near-null result is weakly interesting, not informative either way.

C2.why: Riboformer, RiboMIMO, DeepRibo and Translatomer model ribosome profiling with open code, but none on this species or label.

C3.why: Diversity angle (non-model pathogen, transfer-RNA modification) is real, but the signal is absent in the deposited data.

C4.why: Ribosome profiling is expensive lab work, but a 3%-variance predictor would not replace it.

C5.why: Obvious dummy baselines (global mean, per-expression-bin mean) exist; no published number for this exact task.

D1.why: Open-weight DNA language models (DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA, Nucleotide Transformer) and ESM-2 for proteins all fit coding sequences.

D2.why: Only 3,775 coding sequences to embed once on CPU, then a linear head; no GPU needed.

D3.why: DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA are Apache-2.0; ESM-2 is MIT. No licence blocks this use.

E1.why: Operon/chromosomal-block holdout prevents neighbouring-gene leakage; coordinates are in the files, verified.

E2.why: Hundreds of chromosomal blocks and operons across the 6.5 Mb genome; plenty of groups to hold out.

E3.why: Global mean and per-expression-decile mean are trivially computable; I used the global mean in the ridge cross-validation.

E4.why: Measured it: split-half reliability of the translation-efficiency change is Pearson r = 0.55, so about 30% of variance is explainable.

E5.why: Positive controls available: recover the paper's tryptophan-codon effect, and predict gene length or GC content from codon features.

E6.why: Ran it: shuffling labels collapsed cross-validated R-squared to about 0, as it should.

E7.why: Searched; found no second delta-miaA translatome dataset in any bacterium to validate against.

E8.why: The paper's codon-occupancy numbers need per-codon read coverage, which the gene-level deposit does not contain.

G1.why: Identifiers are PA14 locus tags plus genome coordinates; RefSeq/UniProt mapping has to be built (I did it by coordinates).

G2.why: BACTOME holds transcriptomes and phenotypes for hundreds of P. aeruginosa clinical isolates keyed on PA14 gene IDs.

G3.why: One-to-one on locus tag, but I measured about 8% loss (490/5,966) when mapping between the two PA14 annotations.

G4.why: Combination asks whether MiaA-sensitive genes vary across clinical isolates; the paper already reports a version of this for 77 isolates.

H1.why: All 5,966 genes measured; increases and decreases both recorded, no publication bias toward positives.

H2.why: One strain (PA14), one growth state (planktonic, optical density 0.4), one lab, one pipeline.

H3.why: The honest claim can be written precisely as one sentence with a number I measured.

H4.why: Growth conditions, strains and pipeline are spelled out in the methods and in the featureCounts headers.

I1.why: Named users: the Haussler group (Twincore/HZI) and the Dedon transfer-RNA-modification group.

I2.why: A model explaining 3% of variance would not redirect any experiment.

I3.why: Correlation on translation-efficiency change roughly matches 'which genes to test next', but not a decision threshold.

I4.why: A linear regression on 61 codon frequencies is the honest model and it explains 3%; nothing more complex is warranted.

J1.why: Mostly count wrangling plus a small regression; little real modelling, splits or transfer learning.

J2.why: Bacterial translation has textbook expectations (tryptophan/leucine codon effects) that make nonsense easy to spot.

J3.why: A tidy P. aeruginosa translation-efficiency table with a measured noise ceiling is shareable even though the model fails.

J4.why: A one-week budget is easy to state, but nothing forces it; most of the work is already done.

J5.why: Kill condition is statable (R-squared below 0.05 after three days) but no date is committed anywhere.

existing_models.name: Riboformer (transformer that predicts codon-level ribosome density; Nature Communications 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reports accurate codon-resolution ribosome density prediction across conditions and species including bacterial datasets; evaluated on held-out genes/datasets, exact numbers not retrieved
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Separating true translation dynamics from experimental artefacts across laboratories and protocols

existing_models.name: RiboMIMO (multi-input multi-output deep model of full-length ribosome density; PLOS Computational Biology 2021)
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained and tested on Escherichia coli ribosome profiling datasets at codon resolution, held-out genes
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalising across datasets and capturing long-range dependencies in elongation

existing_models.name: DeepRibo (neural network using prokaryotic ribosome profiling signal for gene annotation; Nucleic Acids Research 2019)
existing_models.score_and_split: Gene-annotation task in bacteria, not translation-efficiency change; held-out genome evaluation

existing_models.name: Khaledi et al. 2020 (machine-learning classifier of antibiotic resistance from P. aeruginosa clinical-isolate transcriptomes and genomes, EMBO Molecular Medicine)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported resistance prediction on 414 clinical isolates with cross-validation; different label from ours
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Transferring classifiers to new isolate collections and new antibiotics

backbone.name: DNABERT-2 or HyenaDNA on coding sequences (DNA language models), or ESM-2 on the encoded proteins
backbone.hardware: laptop CPU; about 3,800 coding sequences to embed once
backbone.licence: DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA Apache-2.0; ESM-2 MIT - all permissive

integration.partner_dataset: BACTOME (transcriptomes and phenotypes of hundreds of P. aeruginosa clinical isolates, NAR 2019)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the genes whose translation depends on the MiaA transfer-RNA modification also show the most expression variation across clinical isolates, and does that variation track virulence?

controls.positive_control: Recover the paper's tryptophan-codon stalling effect; and predict gene length or GC content from the same codon features, which must be near-perfect.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling - already run, cross-validated R-squared collapsed to about 0.
controls.external_validation: None found: no second delta-miaA translatome dataset exists in any bacterium, and no codon-resolution coverage is deposited here.

honest_claim_h3: Among 3,775 well-expressed Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 genes measured in a single planktonic culture at optical density 0.4, codon composition explains about 3% of the variance in the change in ribosome-footprint-to-messenger-RNA ratio caused by deleting miaA, against a replicate-based ceiling of roughly 30%.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a gene's codon sequence to predict how much its translation drops when a transfer-RNA-modifying enzyme is deleted.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per gene: the 61 codon frequencies (and optionally a sequence-model embedding) of its coding sequence. I verified 3,775 genes pass an expression filter out of 5,966 measured features.
plain_idea.predict: The change in translation efficiency - ribosome-profiling reads divided by messenger-RNA reads, in the miaA deletion mutant minus wild type - measured by ribosome profiling and 3'-tag RNA sequencing in GEO series GSE322698.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Bacterial translation researchers would learn which sequence features make a gene dependent on a transfer-RNA modification; even a failure quantifies how little of that dependence is readable from codon counts alone.

more_or_better_data.why: Riboformer and RiboMIMO train on codon-resolution ribosome profiling from many Escherichia coli, yeast and human datasets; we have gene-level counts from one knockout contrast with 2-3 replicates in one strain.

confidence_score.why: Replicates do let us estimate per-gene noise (I measured split-half reliability r = 0.55), which those models do not report, but with 3% explained variance a confidence estimate has nothing useful to qualify.

models_beatable.why: They solve a different, higher-resolution task (per-codon density from raw reads) and cannot be run on gene-level counts, so there is no head-to-head comparison to win.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Improving would require reprocessing raw ribosome-profiling reads to codon resolution - excluded by our no-raw-sequencing rule - and no second dataset measures the same quantity the same way.

ml_idea: Predict per-gene change in translation efficiency on miaA deletion in Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 from coding-sequence features (61 codon frequencies, MiaA-dependent U-starting codon content, or a frozen DNA language-model embedding), with operon-block held-out splits. I built and tested exactly this: ridge regression gives cross-validated R-squared 0.027 (Pearson 0.16) on 3,542 genes, Spearman correlation between the change and U-starting codon fraction is only -0.064, and the replicate-based ceiling is r = 0.55 - so the task as posed on the deposited data has almost no learnable signal.

effort.compute_note: Timed, not guessed: building the count matrix, coordinate-mapping the coding sequences, computing codon frequencies and running 5-fold ridge cross-validation together took about 2 seconds of wall clock on a laptop CPU with under 1 GB of RAM. The 3-hour embedding figure is an estimate for running a small DNA language model over 3,775 coding sequences on CPU.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Regress the translation-efficiency change on the 61 codon frequencies and check the correlation with U-starting codon content - I ran it: cross-validated R-squared 0.027, Spearman -0.064. That kills the project in under an hour.

verdict_reason: The data is genuinely clean, public and tiny (3.5 MB of featureCounts tables, 5,966 genes, no duplicates or missing values), and every Part A killer passes - but I ran the project's central check and the signal is not there: codon composition explains 2.7% of the variance in the miaA-dependent change in translation efficiency, and the correlation with MiaA-sensitive U-starting codons is Spearman -0.06 against a replicate ceiling of r = 0.55. The codon-resolution ribosome stalling the paper is actually about is not in the deposited processed data; recovering it means reprocessing raw reads, which our rules exclude, and even then it would remain one knockout contrast in one strain with no external validation set.
